item.title: Congress reacts to Jensen Huang's reinstatement amid national security concerns
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Members of Congress responded with swift, bipartisan fury Monday over the Nvidia board's surprise decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang at the behest of President Donald Trump , opening a new phase of questions about the chipmaking giant and potential national security lapses. Sen. Tim Scott, the outgoing Republican chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, announced that Huang will testify publicly before the panel on Dec. 3. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair, said the Trump administration needs to explain what role U.S. officials played in what she called a “reckless” decision. Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump’s direct involvement with Nvidia’s decision-making “raises serious national security and corruption questions.” “We must investigate these actions,” said Garcia of California. Nvidia was already facing sharp scrutiny from Congress after Huang acknowledged a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. officials believed to be a spy. Putting Huang back in charge, after Trump said the board did “what we wanted them to do,” raised stark concerns over the administration's role in the company that is central to the AI economy . As Democrats prepare to take charge of Congress in January, they are mounting investigations into the Trump administration, particularly Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has close ties with the company. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier this month said he was frustrated by the Commerce Department's delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed, the company whose CEO, Alice Huang, was involved with Jensen Huang. "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” said Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas, the Republican chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee. “Congress has much to investigate,” he said. Huang is expected to appear for two days of interviews with three House committees next week, along with his public hearing at the Senate panel. “The NVIDIA board’s brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," said a joint statement from Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chairman of the House Select Committee on China; Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., chairman of the House Intelligence Committee; and Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. "We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities.” At issue is the sale of chips to China Of concern to Congress is whether Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies, has been selling its chips to China, in violation of export controls as the U.S. tries to protect certain technology that is at the core of the AI race. Earlier this year, members of Congress urged the U.S. Commerce Department to “suspend or reconsider” Nvidia's export licenses to China and to conduct a full national security review, according to a release earlier this month from Warren and a key Republican on the Senate banking committee, Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana. “Since then, NVIDIA has reportedly received approvals to export hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China’s military, all while attempting to influence the debate over chip controls in Washington, D.C.,” they wrote in a statement in November. “NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang’s confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China’s intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer,” the two senators said. Republicans and Democrats are demanding answers While Republican leaders were mostly quiet on Huang’s return to Nvidia, other Republicans spoke more forcefully Monday. Texas Sen. John Cornyn, who lost his seat after Trump endorsed his GOP primary opponent, questioned the company’s comment that the U.S. said there was no security risk. “No national security risk? Based on what?” Cornyn posted. Cornyn asked whether the FBI did a defensive briefing of Huang to conclude there was no risk, “If not, why not?” Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon wrote on social media that the U.S. cannot say it wants to win the AI competition and then give China its best technology. “Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China,” wrote Bacon, who is retiring from Congress. Ahead of the announcement but after Trump’s call for Huang to be reinstated, Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga of Michigan, who lost reelection to a Democrat, posted: “Ummm… she was, and is, a spy. How about we get serious about making sure China doesn’t steal US company technology?” Utah Sen. John Curtis asked similar questions. “Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board?” Curtis asked. “And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” Democrats add to their anti-corruption agenda Democrats are preparing to dive more deeply into questions of national security and political corruption in Washington as they take over the committee gavels in January. “The guy who was having an affair with a Chinese spy while working relentlessly to help China get access to as many AI chips as possible? Really?” posted Delaware Sen. Chris Coons, who is poised to become the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee when Democrats take the majority. Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a Democrat, said that Congress should investigate “what stock positions took place before the announcement.” Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, who will chair the Senate finance committee and serves on the Senate intelligence committee, said Huang's restatement shows that under Trump and his administration, “our national security is for sale.” “In January, Democrats will hold this corrupt administration accountable,” Wyden said. ___ Associated Press writers Kevin Freking, Aamer Madhani, Joey Cappelletti and Chris Rugaber contributed to this report. item.title: Trump says Huang is not a national security risk. Why are others so concerned?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
When news broke Monday that Nvidia had reinstated Jensen Huang as its president and CEO less than two weeks after he resigned amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs — including one with a woman suspected of spying for China — President Trump was quick to reassure the public that "the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security." "People say, 'Is it a threat to have him?' No, it's a threat to lose him," Trump told CNBC shortly after the announcement . But not everyone agrees . Before Huang resigned, the Trump administration's own intelligence officials reportedly identified Alice Huang — the Chinese-born leader of a Southeast Asian company called Megaspeed — as a Chinese intelligence asset who kept in touch with Beijing's top spy agency for more than a year while she targeted the Nvidia chief. Why does this matter? Without government authorization, U.S. export controls prohibit Nvidia from selling certain advanced AI microchips — the chips that have powered the artificial intelligence boom — directly to China, America's main AI competitor. But during a period when Jensen and Alice Huang were seen dining and socializing together , Megaspeed wound up buying billions of dollars' worth of those same Nvidia chips. And Megaspeed not only has ties to Beijing . It's actually under federal investigation for potentially smuggling advanced Nvidia semiconductors out of the U.S. and into China. Jensen Huang during the Nvidia GTC global AI conference in San Jose, Calif., on March 17, 2026. Carlos Barria/Reuters As a result, Huang's reinstatement triggered immediate bipartisan backlash. Outgoing Republican Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska accused Huang of being "compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy" and said "Nvidia should have moved on" without him. "Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China," Bacon wrote on social media . "We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible." Jensen Huang was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy. Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang. Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China. We cannot say we… — Rep. Don Bacon 🇺🇸✈️🏍️⭐️🎖️ (@RepDonBacon) November 23, 2026 Sen. John Cornyn — another retiring Republican lawmaker — questioned Trump's seemingly cavalier attitude toward Huang and China. "No national security risk?" Cornyn posted . "Based on what?" Democrat Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is set to take over the Senate banking committee in January, posted on X, “This reckless decision to bring back Jensen Huang does not change the fact that Huang and NVIDIA still owe Congress answers.” She said Trump needs to explain what "input" was given and by which senior officials to support Huang’s reinstatement. On Monday, Trump took credit for Huang's return, saying he had spoken directly to Nvidia's board. "I convinced them," the president told CNBC . "I made the deal." The U.S. position on chip sales to China has seesawed over the last 18 months. In April 2025, the Trump administration imposed its first major restrictions on AI semiconductor sales outside the U.S., toughening rules created by the Biden administration. But after several meetings between Trump and Huang — who consistently lobbied for letting chip companies do business with China — the administration eventually approved sales of Nvidia's second-most-powerful chip to Beijing. At the same time, " advisers to Trump told him on at least two occasions that U.S. intelligence had uncovered Ms. Huang's links to the Chinese spy agency and that she was in a close relationship with Mr. Huang while he was still running Nvidia," according to the New York Times . But Trump "downplayed the concerns" and refused to intervene because he "regarded Mr. Huang as a valuable ally and Nvidia as essential to the health of the American economy and stock market," U.S. officials with direct knowledge of the briefings told the paper. Meanwhile, After Jensen stepped down, Trump went on to muse about his return and question whether Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, denying that anyone in his government had ever told him that. "I don't know that she is a spy," the president told reporters last week . "Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy." On Sunday, Trump called for Huang's return on social media. The New York Times reported that it came after "several days of maneuvering to provide the company's board with assurances that Mr. Huang was not facing criminal charges and did not pose a national security risk." That maneuvering reportedly included directing Vice President JD Vance, who has close ties to Silicon Valley, to speak with both Huang and Nvidia's board. President Trump and Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, interact during the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 19, 2025. Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters On Monday, the board announced that it had voted unanimously to reinstate Huang. Trump responded by calling Huang "a Great Patriot and National Treasure" and insisting that "the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." In the same post, Trump added that "NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security." But an internal probe is unlikely to satisfy Congress. Huang is already set to deliver closed-door testimony on Dec. 1 before three congressional committees led by Republicans — and Democrats have signaled that they will keep investigating the issue when they take control of the House and Senate next year. On Monday, Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona accused Trump of "selling out our national security to keep the stock market high." Another Democrat, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, said on social media that "this is the greed and lack of accountability that the country just rejected." "There are serious national security concerns being raised about Jensen Huang that should not be papered over by this administration or the Nvidia board," Pritzker added. The president is a significant investor in Nvidia stock. Last week, the Washington Post reported that by August 2026, Trump held a $13 million to $62 million stake in Nvidia — up from as little as $615,000 at the end of 2024. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also accused the commerce department, led by Howard Lutnick, of stalling efforts by the treasury, defense and state departments, as well as the U.S. trade representative, to block chip sales to Megaspeed. "Commerce has the pen," Bessent said on CNBC earlier this month . "You will have to ask them about their internal processes." Lutnick's former firm Cantor Fitzgerald — now led by his sons — has business relationships with Southeast Asian data centers, leading lawmakers on both sides of the aisle to question "whether Lutnick compromised national security to make money for his family," according to the Guardian . Lutnick should have taken "the threats of communist China more seriously," Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas told the Wall Street Journal last week . Congressional Democrats have said they plan to investigate Lutnick in 2027. item.title: Trump blasts Newsom's death penalty commutations as 'shocking act of injustice'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump listens as Sandy Friend speaks about her late son Michael Lyons, at the Department of Justice in Washington on Nov. 23, 2026. (Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein) WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump blasted Gov. Gavin Newsom's decision to commute every death sentence in California , calling the move "one of the most shocking acts of injustice our country has ever seen" at a Monday press conference with victims' family members at the Department of Justice. Trump said he "couldn't believe" Newsom's choice to commute the sentences of some of California's most notorious serial killers and rapists. He used a good portion of the event to describe in great detail some of the murders that landed the 548 condemned people in California on death row, specifically mentioning Charles Ng, who was convicted of murdering nine adults and two children in 1984-85, Randy Kraft, a serial murderer known in the 1970s and ‘80s as the "Scorecard Killer" and Robert Boyd Rhoades, who brutally raped, tortured and killed 8-year-old Michael Lyons in 1996, among others. "You'd have to read their biographies to see how bad they were. Some of them you wouldn't even believe," Trump said, calling Newsom a "terrible governor." "He stood with the murderers and the child slayers," he said. "But today we say the American people stand with you." Trump's press conference seemed designed as much to politically whack Newsom over the commutations as it was to honor victims, representing the latest chapter in the years-long feud between the two men who have regularly sparred during their overlapping time in office over crime and punishment. Newsom, for his part, said his commutations decision, which he announced earlier this month, was inspired in part by a national reckoning over the death penalty, including a botched execution in Tennessee and a Trump administration announcement - later walked back - that it planned to livestream a federal execution by a firing squad. Newsom slammed Trump in a video he posted just before the press conference, calling out the president for what he claimed was blatant hypocrisy. He said Trump has used his post to pardon numerous criminals, including those with close ties to the president or his allies. Trump also granted widespread clemency to nearly all of the Jan. 6 defendants , many of whom went on to reoffend . "Donald Trump doesn't oppose mercy. He sells it," Newsom said. "If you are poor, Black or brown, you get the needle. If you are rich and know Donald Trump, you get a pardon and a personal phone call." Newsom noted that in 1989, Trump called for the death penalty for the so-called Central Park Five, or the five Black and Latino teenagers who were wrongfully convicted of raping a white woman in the park. "They were innocent, DNA proved it, you never apologized," Newsom said. Both Newsom and Trump have touted crime statistics to promote their agendas and policy priorities. Trump said during the event that " crime rates have gone down 84%," though it was unclear what specific crimes he was referencing or if it was an overall national or local trend. Newsom's office has in recent weeks also touted lower crimes in California, including a "record low" homicide rate . Trump's event underscores the intense scrutiny and political backlash that has surrounded Newsom since he made his decision, which already faces at least one legal challenge and that in some cases must be reviewed under state law by the California Supreme Court. But the president's choice to orchestrate such a major event to publicly admonish a governor's decision is unusual, said Erwin Chemerinsky, dean of UC Berkeley Law School. "I do not recall a president ever attempting to undermine a governor's commuting of death sentences," Chemerinsky said in an email. "Other governors have done this, but to my knowledge, no president ever has done this before." That's in part because, however controversial, governors have legal jurisdiction over state commutations so Trump has little, if any, power to stop Newsom's action. "This is a publicity stunt by the president, not a serious legal effort," Chemerinsky said. Several family members of victims also spoke at the event, during which they celebrated Trump and ridiculed Newsom. "Michael was 8 years old. He loved his sisters, fishing, Ninja Turtles, telling campfire stories and bringing me flowers. Michael was afraid of the dark. He believed the boogeyman was going to get him," his mother, Sandy Friend said, battling tears. Friend said the night her son was killed, "Michael learned that the boogeyman was real." She said Newsom, with the swipe of a pen and without notifying families, "erased" justice for her son's killer. "You took the only justice we had and let families feel abandoned by the state that promised to protect us," she said. "You'll never understand the unimaginable pain that you're putting these families through. Face me, Governor Newsom. Tell me Michael's life doesn't matter." Newsom was careful to focus his criticism on Trump and did not use the video to explain his decision or undermine victims' grief. In an open letter to Californians announcing the commutations, Newsom said he agonized over it for years and ultimately made his choice over a firm belief that "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values." He also told the Chronicle in an interview earlier this month that he made the choice after speaking with the sisters of Polly Klaas , a 12-year-old who was abducted from her home in Petaluma in 1993 and brutally killed. The man convicted of murdering her was sentenced to death and is still alive. "This decision was not made by a jury. It was not approved by the voters. It was made by one politician acting alone," Marc Klaas, Polly's father, said at the event. "While nothing can bring Polly back, her life mattered. The pain inflicted on our family was real." Newsom acknowledged the families who joined Trump's press conference to denounce the commutations in his Monday video. "To the families standing with him today, your grief is real," he said. "That's why every person, every person, on California's former death row will die in prison. No one walks out. Donald Trump's criminals? They walk out." Speculation had swirled for weeks that Newsom would commute the sentences before he leaves office in January and before launching an expected 2028 presidential bid. The decision could help Newsom earn support from the more progressive wing of his party in what's expected to be a crowded Democratic primary field, but it could also hobble his odds against more law-and-order candidates who appeal to anti-MAGA Republicans and swing voters. The White House emphasized that California voters have repeatedly rejected efforts to overturn the death penalty, including as early as 2016, when they voted against a ballot measure to ban it and passed another to speed up executions, part of which was later invalidated by the courts. National support for the death penalty also remains strong. A July 2026 survey by the Pew Research Center found that two-thirds of American adults support capital punishment for people convicted of murder, including 51% of Democrats and 84% of Republicans. Trump touted an executive order he signed on his first day back in office "restoring the death penalty" after former President Joe Biden commuted the sentences of 37 people on federal death row during his last days in office. Trump also announced Monday he would sign a directive "ordering the Department of Justice to seek the death penalty for child murderers, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims," adding that the order would also "expedite the execution of federal death sentences." It's unclear how or whether the order would affect California and Newsom's commutations, which are within his jurisdiction as governor. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for clarification. Trump also said Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, would introduce a bill to "strengthen the death penalty in America." "And it's going to be much different than it was in the past," Trump said. "It's going to be strong and it'll be swift." Natasha Minsker, a lobbyist who has worked with a coalition of anti-death penalty advocates urging Newsom to commute the sentences, slammed Trump for using the death penalty for "political purposes" in a way that doesn't help victims or their families. "It is once again prosecutors and politicians using the death penalties to bring attention to themselves and for their own political gain and with no eye to what's in the best interest of the families and with no interest to what actually protects our communities and keeps us safe," she said. "This is a state law issue. This is about whether people in California support the governor, and it's about the governor's ability to commute under the state Constitution." This article originally published at Trump blasts Newsom's death penalty commutations as ‘shocking act of injustice' . item.title: Judge pushed back on DOJ over search of Ilhan Omar's home, court records show
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — A magistrate judge who authorized a recent search of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar 's home by federal agents ruled that the Minnesota Democrat was entitled to assert her right to privacy protections afforded to sitting members of Congress at the outset of the search, according to court documents unsealed on Monday. The unsealed filings reveal how Justice Department attorneys and U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh resolved their initial disagreement over the thorny constitutional implications of searching a member of Congress’ private residence for a criminal investigation. The heavily redacted documents — released in response to a lawsuit filed by media organizations — do not appear to shed new light on the reason or outcome of the search itself or disclose new details of an immigration-fraud investigation that Omar claims is politically motivated. Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, The Associated Press reported last month, citing a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The unsealed filings show that Sharbaugh — before authorizing the search of Omar's home — raised concerns about the “Speech or Debate Clause” implications of searching a private residence belonging to a member of Congress. The clause, which is designed to protect legislators from executive branch interference or intimidation, includes a privilege against compelled disclosures. Sharbaugh said he disagreed with the government's argument that the privilege is limited only to official congressional offices and certain electronic devices. “That logic does not hold,” the magistrate wrote. Sharbaugh concluded that the government's law-enforcement interests needed to be balanced against Omar's constitutional rights as a member of Congress. He said the government ultimately agreed to a search protocol allowing Omar to invoke a privilege over any Speech or Debate Clause material before agents carried out the search. Omar, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in Somalia, has been a target of anti-immigrant rhetoric by President Donald Trump and many Republican allies. She hasn’t been charged with any crimes and has denied any wrongdoing. Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the partial unsealing of court filings related to the Oct. 12 search of Omar’s Washington, D.C., home by Department of Homeland Security agents. He ruled after over a dozen news organizations, including The Associated Press, argued that the public has a First Amendment right to access the records. Boasberg agreed with the government that it would be premature to unseal a 67-page search warrant affidavit containing sensitive details of the government’s investigation. In a court filing last month, the government argued that it would jeopardize the investigation to unseal the court records before a charging decision is made. An attorney for Omar didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment Monday on the unsealed documents. Agents conducted the court-authorized search less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Omar won her reelection bid. The Justice Department historically has avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of an election. Omar has said DHS agents seized 17 items , including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift. ___ Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/records-government-judge-debated-constitutional-031911746.html

item.title: Army will detonate bomb-making material on Wednesday after court clears way
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The U.S. Army plans to detonate 68 barrels of toxic lead-based explosives stored at a facility in Iowa on Wednesday morning after securing approval from a federal appeals court. The Army said in a statement Monday that multiple agencies were in agreement that it should proceed with the “carefully controlled detonation” and that the current governor of Iowa, Kim Reynolds, the governor-elect, Rob Sand say “the call belongs to the experts.” “This is a consensus decision,” acting Army Secretary Adam Telle posted on social media . The announcement followed a judgment from the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals earlier on Monday, which said the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency had demonstrated it had “adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead dust.” The ruling acknowledged the detonation presented ”real risks,” but concluded, “However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place.” The court’s decision came hours after President Trump announced that he had halted the plan, another twist in an ongoing controversy over the military's effort to dispose of the volatile material before it potentially detonates on its own. Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday morning that, while he believes the "proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem," he would not allow the Army to destroy the material until federal courts sign off on the plan and Sand gives his approval. Sand, who takes office in January, has said the decision is up to the Trump administration “based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago.” The explosion threatens to send a plume of toxic lead dust over local communities, livestock and farmland in the surrounding area. Environmentalists sued to stop the detonation last week, setting off a back-and-forth legal battle. The military has argued that the controlled detonation must take place soon, before impending cold weather potentially causes the material to combust on its own. Here's what led to the current situation, what the dangers are and what might happen next. How did we get here? The roots of the controversy reportedly date back to at least March, when the Army discovered nearly 5 tons of deteriorating lead azide, a dangerous bomb-making material, stored at an ammunition plant in rural Iowa. According to legal filings , the lead azide had crystallized over the course of two decades, leaving it highly susceptible to exploding. The material is so volatile, the Army says, that the friction and motion of attempting to move it somewhere safer would likely cause it to explode. According to the New York Times, the Army at first hired a chemical company to carry out a process that could neutralize the material without an explosion, but later determined that detonating it was the right course of action. Earlier this month, the Environmental Protection Agency approved an emergency permit allowing the Army to carry out a controlled detonation of the lead azide. The detonation was initially scheduled to take place on Friday. But local environmental groups filed a lawsuit aiming to stop the plan from going forward, arguing that the EPA failed to apply proper environmental standards when it approved the detonation, creating the risk of "immediate, irreparable harm" to surrounding communities. On Thursday, a federal appeals court issued an order temporarily blocking the Army from carrying out the detonation. But the Army argued in a filing Saturday that the situation has become so dangerous that it has the authority to proceed under a separate emergency exemption. The blast was on track to happen on Wednesday until Trump intervened. The court issued its ruling allowing the detonation to proceed about five hours after Trump's post was published. What are the risks? Lead is a neurotoxin that poses a serious risk to those who are exposed to it, particularly pregnant women and young children. No one disputes that blowing up the barrels of lead azide could release dangerous material to the surrounding area. The Army shared modeling showing lead particles from the explosion traveling as far as 40 miles and airborne dust drifting up to 100 miles. The American Lung Association has advised people in the area to stay indoors for 24 to 48 hours after the blast to avoid exposure. The Army argues that, whatever risks the planned detonation poses, doing nothing creates the danger of something much worse. An aerial view shows homes on November 20, 2026 in Middletown, Iowa. Scott Olson/Getty Images) The real choice … is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion," the government wrote in a legal filing . But environmental groups have countered that the public was only given a few days' notice before the initial planned detonation, not nearly enough time for local residents to understand the full scope of the risk and take the steps they need to stay safe. The groups also questioned how the Army allowed the situation to become so urgent when it had been aware of the material for at least eight months. Sand echoed that sentiment in a post on social media on Sunday. "No good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been," he wrote on X . "Most clearly, since a contract to remove explosive risk was signed this spring, we must all be asking why it was cancelled, why nothing was done, and why we are rushing to demolition now in late November." item.title: Hegseth's ex-chief of staff calls on him to resign over Iran war and Pentagon missteps
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The former top aide to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is calling on him to resign, saying he has badly mismanaged both the Pentagon and ongoing war in Iran, and let showmanship get in the way of doing his job well. “Pete’s ability to be effective has been constrained and very soon he’ll have lost any ability to be effective,” Joe Kasper, who was chief of staff to Hegseth for the first three months of the Trump administration, told POLITICO. “For that reason and others it’s time for Pete to call it quits.” In a nearly hourlong interview, Kasper critiqued Hegseth’s tenure as secretary, assailing his choice to fire top military leaders as well as senior Black and female military brass , his obsession with image and his handling of the Iran war, which he called a “shitshow.” He also said there was no evidence that several Pentagon officials who were fired last year for allegedly leaking to the media ever shared material without authorization to reporters. “Pete’s been belligerent in his stewardship of an office that will outlive him or any memory of his service,” Kasper said. A senior Pentagon official, speaking on behalf of the Defense Department, said in a statement to POLITICO that it wasn’t surprising that a “disgruntled former staffer—someone who could barely survive ninety days in the building—is now peddling made up gossip to the media.” “Secretary Hegseth is laser focused on restoring lethality to the force and supporting our warfighters, while Mr. Kasper is more focused on rewriting history to cover for his own failed tenure,” the official said. President Donald Trump said he was keeping Hegseth as the Pentagon’s leader amid speculation by senior administration officials and other Republicans about Hegseth's standing in the administration. The party’s losses in the midterms were attributed by some in part to the ongoing war in Iran. Hegseth’s footing in the administration has also been helped by the elevation of his ally Stephen Miller to be White House chief of staff. Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) recently wrote in his memoir that his deciding vote to confirm Hegseth was the “biggest regret of my career,” and even Trump ally Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) said several weeks ago that he had “no idea” what Hegseth’s Iran strategy was. While Hegseth survived a House impeachment vote earlier this month, he could face another attempt in the next Congress when Democrats assume control of both chambers. By calling for his resignation, Kasper, an Air Force veteran, said he wanted to “speak truth to power” after a sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier admonished people around Hegseth to stop laughing during a ceremony on Veterans Day. The viral video led Hegseth to award the sentinel a Joint Service Commendation Medal. Kasper said the award was an “attempt to trivialize” the moment, as “if that makes it all okay.” A former chief of staff to disgraced former Rep. Duncan D. Hunter (R-Calif.), Kasper said he first met Hegseth around 2010 when Hegseth headed up Concerned Veterans for America and Kasper was on Capitol Hill. Kasper would later work at the Department of Homeland Security, the Navy and the Air Force in the first Trump administration. His critics said last year in a New York Magazine story that Kasper quickly ran into trouble in his new role at the Pentagon. The magazine said that he was often late to meetings and developed a reputation for not fully carrying out critical tasks. Kasper told the publication that some of the criticism was “arbitrary and subjective.” After departing the chief of staff role, Kasper was a special government employee at the Pentagon for a time, working on the Defense Department’s advisory boards. Since leaving his full-time job at the department, he has been a principal at Ervin Graves Strategy Group, advising clients on defense issues, and is chair of the advisory board of the publicly-traded rare earths company REalloys. During his stint at the Pentagon in 2025, Kasper was a leading figure in the firings of senior adviser Dan Caldwell, Hegseth deputy chief of staff Darin Selnick and Colin Carroll, chief of staff to Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg. The trio were ousted in April 2025 amid a leak investigation. At the time, they denied disclosing sensitive information without authorization. Kasper told POLITICO that he now believes there was no evidence that they had ever leaked anything, an assertion backed up by the New York Times , which reported that an internal investigation into leaks didn’t find any wrongdoing on the part of the three men. Earlier this year, Caldwell rejoined the administration in the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. Kasper had requested an investigation into Defense Department leaks in March 2025, which related to the development of military plans to “reclaim” the Panama Canal, Elon Musk’s visit to the Pentagon and a temporary pause in the collection of intelligence for Ukraine. Kasper left his role as Hegseth’s chief of staff soon after his colleagues were ousted. Hegseth said Kasper had not been fired and expressed support for him. “Joe is a great guy, great American,” Hegseth told Fox News at the time . “He has done a fantastic job for us at the Defense Department. … You make changes over time, and we’re grateful for everything Joe’s done.” In recounting his issues with Hegseth, Kasper also predicted that it would be impossible for the combative Hegseth to work with Congress or get proper funding for department priorities. “He’s not just burned bridges up on the Hill,” he said. “He’s napalmed them. … He’s going to be suffocated, and it’s not like it’s going to be a slow suffocation. It’s going to be a quick asphyxiation.” Kasper said that he realized within a week of starting at the Pentagon that Hegseth’s focus was “all about Pete rather than the institution and the men and women who support it.” “There’s quite an emphasis on the showmanship,” he said. “The virtues of humility and basically service before self and those things have disappeared. I didn’t see those at the start, and see them ever less so now.” Hegseth “overindulged in ego, in attitude, and in entitlement,” he said. Kasper called Hegseth’s promotion of issues like measuring soldiers’ testosterone “distractions,” saying it was “silly” how an early emphasis on bringing back the warrior ethos and an increased prioritization of recruiting and retention standards had devolved into a measure of how many jumping jacks and push-ups a soldier could do. Kasper also said that the Pentagon’s senior leadership had been hollowed out by the removal or resignations of many top leaders, including Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, Army Chief of Staff Randy George, and Gen. Christopher T. Donahue, the top Army general in Europe . Driscoll left after months of tensions with Hegseth; the Pentagon didn’t give official reasons for forcing George and Donahue to retire early. “These are real inspirational figureheads who were committed to the mission, but publicly they were treated in ways that would have made you think otherwise,” Kasper said, adding it was disrespectful to treat them poorly after many had dedicated their lives to serving the country. He called the Army “essentially leaderless,” adding: “At almost every high-profile position, or every senior leader position, there’s a vacancy.” Kasper said that Hegseth would rank close to the bottom 10% of defense secretaries in American history. “I think history will be much crueler to him than I could be,” he said. item.title: Democrats to hold a dozen 2028 presidential primary debates starting in June
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The debate stage is prepared for the sixth Democratic primary debate of the 2020 presidential campaign season in Los Angeles on 19 December 2019. Photograph: Robyn Beck/AFP/Getty Images The Democratic National Committee (DNC) unveiled on Monday its plans to hold a dozen 2028 presidential primary debates over 10 months, with the first set to take place in June. Between June 2027 and March 2028, the DNC will host 12 debates, allowing up to 20 candidates to participate , so long as they agree to new criteria. That includes pledging to reject “dark money” – or funding from outside groups that do not disclose their donors – and not participating in unsanctioned debates. The announcement came just weeks after Democrats swept the midterm elections and won majorities in the House, Senate and governor’s offices. “Democrats are on offense after our historic victories in the midterms, and the DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle ,” Ken Martin, the DNC chair, said in a statement. “The fair and transparent process and experienced leadership team we’re announcing today will keep our party united, strengthen our eventual nominee, and put Democrats in position to take back the White House.” Though no candidates have officially announced their 2028 presidential bid, the Democratic field is expected to be large. Several names have been floated as potential contenders, including Gavin Newsom, the governor of California; Kamala Harris, the former vice-president and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee; Josh Shapiro, the governor of Pennsylvania; JB Pritzker, the governor of Illinois; Andy Beshear, the governor of Kentucky, and more. But early polling among Democratic primary voters shows that party members would more likely support a younger and more progressive candidate. In an Emerson College Poll , 17% of respondents said they would support Jon Ossoff, the Georgia senator, while 12% said they would support the New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll , 29% of respondents believed Pete Buttigieg , the former secretary of transportation, and Ossoff would make excellent presidential candidates. Ocasio-Cortez has not announced any plans to run for president, but progressive organizers are hopeful she’ll throw her hat into the ring. Recently, hundreds of organizers from Ready for AOC , a new group, held a Zoom call to try to convince Ocasio-Cortez to launch a presidential campaign. Buttigieg similarly has not announced a campaign, but allies of the former transportation secretary are launching a grassroots effort to try to inspire him to make a second bid for president, Politico reported. Given how large the primary field may be, the DNC said early debates may be held over two consecutive nights, in which qualifying candidates will randomly be assigned a night to participate. Like in past primaries, candidates who qualify for the primary will need to meet certain polling criteria among other qualifications. The DNC said it would announce its specific criteria for the first two debates in January, but that it will include measures to reflect a candidate’s support, such as grassroots funding. Among other new features, the DNC’s debates will incorporate “creators and influencers” in the process, though they did not elaborate on what their role may be. The DNC will release more information in January about the dates, locations and media partners of the first two debates. item.title: ICE arrested his wife as they boarded a flight. Now he's pleading for her release.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The husband of a woman whose arrest by immigration agents inside a jetway at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport gained national attention says he felt "useless" when seeing his wife and father-in-law be taken into federal custody, calling the episode "unjust." Jose Castillo, an American citizen, teared up when recounting the moment on Saturday when masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers detained his wife, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, and his father-in-law, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza. "You black out. You don't even know what's going on. You don't even know what's happening. Everything is moving so fast. Trying to protect your wife and they're taking your father-in-law," Castillo told CBS News in an interview Monday. "As a U.S. citizen, you feel useless." Castillo said he felt "disgusted." "How can you sit with yourself and strip somebody away like that in broad daylight, in front of families?" Castillo added. The arrest was captured on videos that have gone viral. Hernandez Mejia is heard wailing and saying she has a valid work permit, while bystanders demand answers from the federal agents. Department of Homeland Security officials identified Hernandez Mejia and Larrondo Mendoza as Mexican nationals living in the U.S. illegally after overstaying their visas. The agency said ICE officers were targeting Larrondo Mendoza for arrest when "other passengers began obstructing federal officers." DHS accused Hernandez Mejia of assaulting agents, alleging she threw hot coffee on them. Castillo pushed back on the allegations. "There was no assault on her end," Castillo said. "She did nothing. She was being shoved. They came directly at us." "When you're coming at me and my wife and you're shoving us, obviously coffee's going to be spilled," he added. DHS has said Hernandez Mejia "will be charged with assaulting a federal officer." Castillo said he was traveling with his wife and father-in-law to a family event when they were approached by ICE agents in plainclothes on the jetway to an Alaska Airlines flight. The flight was delayed by over two hours, and the flight crew had to be replaced, the airline said. Officials at Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle, which runs the airport, said they were not given prior notice of the ICE operation. The Port of Seattle said it was "outraged." Hernandez Mejia and her father remain in ICE custody in Tacoma, Washington, according to their attorney. Castillo pleaded for their release. "They don't deserve to be in there," he said. "It was done in such an unjust manner." The incident is the latest in a string of ICE operations that have gone awry in recent weeks, even after President Trump acknowledged to 60 Minutes that his crackdown on illegal immigration may have been "too tough." Last week, video captured ICE agents pushing a pregnant woman and U.S. citizen to the ground in Modesto, California. ICE accused her of interfering with the arrest of a man with a criminal record. In Texas, an ICE agent is facing criminal charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after allegedly striking a Mexican immigrant with an unmarked SUV. His attorney has called the incident an "accident." The detention at Sea-Tac airport is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to send ICE officers to major airports across the country to arrest travelers who are in the U.S. illegally or with a tenuous legal status. Those arrested have included travelers with pending legal immigration applications but whose underlying permission to be in the U.S. expired. Olia Catala, who is representing the father and daughter detained at Sea-Tac, said her clients entered the U.S. as tourists and that both have pending immigration applications. Hernandez Mejia, Catala said, applied for a green card as the spouse of a U.S. citizen. She said the family was trying to follow the immigration process prior to being arrested. "Congress created legal pathways and Sofia and her father were using them," Catala said. "We can't tell immigrants to use the legal pathways, to follow the law and then punish them for doing just that." This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ice-arrest-seattle-airport-husband/

item.title: White House staffer reportedly reveals Smithsonian overhaul plans by accident
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(AFP via Getty) The Trump administration's plans for the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History were accidentally discovered by a commuter on a Washington Metro train last month. A commuter spotted a document titled "Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan" displayed on a staffer's laptop, snapped photos, and sent them to ProPublica, the outlet reported . The list includes 25 items, including firing the museum's director, Anthea Hartig, and several top administrators and curators; installing a new permanent exhibit called "The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance;" creating an exhibit on "Great Families of American History;" and announcing a new "colossus statue" of George Washington for the museum's entrance. The plan also calls for new guidelines for interpreting exhibits and a review of the Smithsonian's strategy for traveling exhibitions, including blocking one underway called "The Bias Inside Us." The Smithsonian's financial grants to "woke third parties" would also be reviewed, and its online K-12 curriculum would be overhauled to "realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology." The plan appears to be a work in progress. The staffer also wrote down other proposals on a sheet of paper in plain view, according to ProPublica. The outlet identified the staffer as Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office that produced the July report. The White House did not respond to ProPublica's request for comment. The Trump administration has been at odds with the Smithsonian since the president's second term began. President Donald Trump issued an executive order in July directing the Interior Department, through the National Park Service, to install temporary signs along sidewalks and walkways leading to the museum, warning visitors that the museum does not accurately present U.S. history. The order said the signs "shall notify visitors that the Museum exhibits should be renovated consistent with the findings in the Report and direct visitors to locations and resources for accurate information regarding America's history." Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch announced his resignation in September. The Smithsonian operates outside the executive branch, and museum directors report to the secretary, who is subject to oversight by a board of regents that includes Vice President JD Vance, Chief Justice John Roberts, a bipartisan group of lawmakers, and citizen regents. item.title: Jensen Huang is back. Now comes the hard part: Fresh scrutiny in D.C.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Returning Jensen Huang to Nvidia's top job was hailed in Silicon Valley as essential to the future of the AI trade, and on Monday his supporters got their wish. But the embattled CEO's road back to the job may prove easier than the one awaiting him in Washington. Huang's reinstatement comes less than two weeks after revelations of his relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative forced his resignation, setting off a political firestorm over Nvidia's dealings with China and its influence within the Trump administration. Now back atop the company he co-founded more than three decades ago, Huang faces a growing list of congressional inquiries, federal and state scrutiny, and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle demanding answers about whether his relationship compromised US national security. "All the questions that people have been raising in the press and in social media, all those questions are still out there," Martijn Rasser, vice president of technology leadership at the Special Competitive Studies Project (SCSP), told Yahoo Finance. "That aspect of the story is still very much in play," said Rasser, a former officer at the Central Intelligence Agency and former director of the technology and national security program at the Center for a New American Security. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks after attending the AI Ecosystem Reception in Tokyo, Japan, on July 16, 2026. (Reuters/Manami Yamada/File Photo) Reuters / REUTERS Nvidia's board of directors said on Monday that the decision to reinstate Huang came after they "received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk." President Trump, who had pushed for Huang's reinstatement since his ouster on Nov. 12, confirmed that he had called the company's board of directors to personally lobby for Huang, telling CNBC that he had been speaking to the board "directly and indirectly" and had offered assurances on national security. The president noted in a Truth Social post that the US government "has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security," and that "the Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." Lawmakers, including prominent members from the president's own party, have disputed those assertions. Republican Sen. John Cornyn, who sits on the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee and the Select Committee on Intelligence, wrote shortly after the news broke Monday, "No national security risk? Based on what?" Republican Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter last week requesting Huang's testimony before their respective House committees, saying that "recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information." Democrats made similar calls on Monday, following on prior statements condemning potential national security violations at Nvidia ( NVDA ). "This reckless decision to bring back Jensen Huang does not change the fact that Huang and NVIDIA still owe Congress answers," Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, wrote on Monday . "Huang's return only increases the urgency to pass bipartisan export control bills and make sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk." Read more: Thinking of buying Nvidia stock? Consider also buying dozens just like it. In a similar tone to Cornyn, Delaware Democratic Sen. Chris Coons wrote on X , "No national security risk? The guy who was having an affair with a Chinese spy while working relentlessly to help China get access to as many AI chips as possible? Really?" Calls for change at Nvidia came from inside the White House as well, despite the president's statements. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News last week that Nvidia's board needed to "go outside the company" as it searched for a new leader, arguing that the company needed a "dramatic shake-up." Bessent, however, softened his tone in interviews on Sunday. Republicans have also pushed on wider questions surrounding the US government's involvement with Nvidia, including coming congressional interrogations of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whom Huang has called "the person I talk to most in the administration." "If Howard Lutnick wanted my support, perhaps he should have responded to my many letters warning about these Chinese communist front companies and, more importantly, taking the threats of communist China more seriously," Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal. Nvidia has said in multiple quarterly reports that it projects no compute revenue from China in forward-looking estimates, stating in its fiscal second quarter report, "Under the current rules and geopolitical landscape, we are unable to create and deliver a competitive product for wide distribution in China's data center market with the approval from both the USG and the Chinese government." Huang's first major test will come next week on Dec. 1, when he is scheduled to appear before three House committees investigating his ties to the suspected Chinese operative, Alice Huang, and the potential diversion of advanced Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is also set to face questioning alongside senior Commerce Department officials responsible for enforcing restrictions on chip exports. An inquiry by the Commerce Department into Singapore-based Megaspeed — the company Alice Huang was once associated with — over alleged violations of US semiconductor export controls was transferred to the Justice Department after Teter asked the Commerce Department for information on the investigation, The New York Times reported." President Trump speaks to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 29, 2026. (Reuters/Kevin Lamarque/File Photo) REUTERS / REUTERS Huang has separately agreed to testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3, setting up an appearance alongside Lutnick, who has also agreed to testify and is facing scrutiny over reports he slowed investigations into companies suspected of funneling controlled semiconductors into China. Amid a feud with Lutnick that has spilled into public light over the past two weeks, Bessent said investigators would need to ask about any potential export control violations by Nvidia or its customers such as Megaspeed, were they "a low-level fail, was it in the middle, or was it up in the C-suite? Who knew?" The controversy has also drawn investigators beyond Capitol Hill. California's attorney general has subpoenaed Nvidia as part of an investigation connected to Huang's affair. The Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating Nvidia over accounting violations , per Reuters. Proposed national legislation could also present further complications for Nvidia's business. The so-called AI Overwatch Act would tighten export controls on shipments of advanced dual-use AI chips to foreign nations such as China, while the Chip Security Act would impose new verification measures on the locations of chips exported abroad. The Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware (MATCH) Act would impose more restrictive export controls on the equipment needed to make advanced AI chips. "I think the news of the past few weeks has underscored in the mind of many legislators on Capitol Hill that not enough is being done to ensure that critical US technologies stay out of the hands of our adversaries," SCSP's Rasser told Yahoo Finance. As Huang prepares to appear before Congress, he will have an important ally in Trump, who has repeatedly referred to Huang as a close associate. The president said on Monday that he personally weighed in on the Nvidia board's decision to reinstate Huang and believes his intervention was "very important" to the decision, telling CNBC, "I convinced them." "If I thought he did something wrong, I wouldn't be recommending to his board to hire him," Trump said. Follow Jake Conley on X @byjakeconley or email him at jake.conley@yahooinc.com . This article originally appeared on Yahoo Finance at https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/jensen-huang-is-back-atop-nvidia-he-has-a-long-road-ahead-in-washington-164747640.html
